title: Stress Test the Plan
briefing: The three-year plan assumes 6% revenue growth and stable costs. Hollis Varga wants to know whether Valtren survives a bad year before the bank renews its loan facility.
Run the stress test and tell the executive what it means.

context.text: Cash is now below 2.5 million after this year's incidents. The bank will look closely.
The board's new appetite statement includes a liquidity floor of 1.5 million cash.

evidence.title: Plan, year 1
evidence.body: Revenue 51.0m. Costs 47.2m. Operating margin 3.8m. Opening cash 3.0m. Other cash outflows in the year: fleet replacement 1.2m, loan repayment 1.0m. Planned year-end cash: 4.6m. Loan covenant: cash must stay above 1.0m.

evidence.title: Proposed stress scenarios
body: S1 Fuel shock: diesel +35% (fuel is 12% of costs).
S2 Client loss: the second-largest client (9% of revenue, 4.59m) leaves at the start of the year. Serving it costs 4.25m, of which 60% can be cut within the year.
S3 Combined: S1 and S2 together.

evidence.title: Management actions available
evidence.body: Fuel surcharge clause (recovers about half of a fuel rise after one quarter). Hiring freeze (saves 0.8m). Defer fleet replacement (frees 1.2m cash).

questions.prompt: What does S1 (fuel +35%) do to the year's operating margin before any action?

options.label: Margin falls by about 1.98m, to about 1.8m
Margin falls by 35%, to about 2.5m
options.feedback: The rise applies to fuel costs, not the margin.

options.label: Margin falls by 5.66m, into a loss of about 1.9m
options.feedback: That is the whole fuel bill, not the 35% increase.

questions.prompt: Under S3 (combined), before management action, what happens to the margin?

options.label: About -0.2m: the margin is wiped out
options.feedback: Client loss: revenue -4.59m, costs cut 0.6 x 4.25m = 2.55m, net -2.04m. Plus fuel -1.98m: 3.8 - 2.04 - 1.98 = -0.22m.

options.label: About +1.8m: the client's costs go with it, so only the fuel shock really bites
About -4.6m: the lost revenue comes straight off the margin
options.feedback: Lost revenue is partly offset by costs that can be cut.

questions.prompt: What is the key conclusion for the executive?

options.label: Year-end cash falls to about 0.6m in S3, below the covenant, unless surcharges and a hiring freeze start in Q1
options.feedback: 3.0 - 0.22 - 2.2 = 0.58m. Surcharges (about 0.7m in the year) and the freeze (0.8m) restore about 2.1m; deferral adds 1.2m if needed.

options.label: Cash stays above the covenant in every scenario, because opening cash and the margin absorb the shocks
options.feedback: S3 leaves about 0.6m at year end, below the covenant.

options.label: S3 breaches the covenant whatever management does, so the loan should be renegotiated now
options.feedback: Too pessimistic: the available actions keep cash above the covenant if taken early.

questions.prompt: How do you make sure the actions happen in time?

options.label: Agree trigger points now (e.g. diesel +15% for two months, or client notice) with named owners
options.feedback: Decisions made in calm are faster and better than decisions made in crisis.

options.label: Keep the actions on file and decide when a scenario starts to happen, with the facts in hand
options.feedback: Delay costs a quarter of recovery, which is the margin of survival here.

options.label: Freeze hiring and defer the fleet now: the cost of acting early is small next to a covenant breach
options.feedback: Costly insurance against a scenario, not a forecast.

questions.prompt: What do you tell the bank?

options.label: Share the stress test, including the combined scenario and the pre-agreed actions
options.feedback: Lenders trust borrowers who show they know their downside.

options.label: Share the base plan and the headline that Valtren has tested its downside
options.feedback: Banks run their own downside; hiding yours costs credibility.

options.label: Answer the bank's questions fully but volunteer nothing beyond the information pack
options.feedback: A missed chance to build trust before a renewal.

lesson: Stress tests matter for the decisions they trigger: quantify the downside, agree triggers and owners in advance, and share the result with those who rely on you.
